newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHLETICS-WORLD CHAMPS IN THE RED AS ATHENS BIDS FOR OLYMPICS.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-WORLD CHAMPS IN THE RED AS ATHENS BIDS FOR OLYMPICS.

text.p: Greece's bid to host the 2004 Olympics will go through its final test during Athens' world athletics championship starting next week with organisers expecting a high-class event but also a huge deficit.

"This is the big one. The eyes of the world are on Athens for the championship one month before the International Olympic Committee votes for the 2004 venue. Athens wants to prove it is the best candidate," a senior government official told Reuters.

The August 1-10 event at Athens' 80,000-seat Olympic Stadium will feature state-of-art facilities, a dazzling opening ceremony, hundreds of VIP guests and 3,000 athletes from 200 countries in action, including some of Atlanta's biggest stars.

Marathon runners will race along the original route, and sprinters will test their strength on a superfast new track in front of a record 3,000 accredited journalists. More than two billion people will watch the event on television every day.

Money prizes will be awarded to athletes for the first time with a $60,000 bonus for gold medalists, $30,000 for silver medalists and $20,000 for the bronze medal. A world record will carry a $100,000 award.
The opening ceremony at Athens' marble Panathinaikon Staium, site of the 1896 first modern Olympics, will include a concert by oscar-winning composer Vangelis with a spectacular special effects show.
"We wanted to make this championship different and bigger than the others held so far. We see it as a mini-Olympics," sports undersecretary Andreas Fouras said.

But vicious divisions among the organisers and a late start in preparation have created a financial nightmare with the final cost expected around $36 million and revenues only $7.3 million, mainly from ticket sales.
The International Amateur Athletics Federation (IAAF) awarded the championship to Athens in March 1995 after Mexico City turned it down because of lack of funds.
The Greek Athletics Federation (SEGAS) agreed to undertake the project with no funding from IAAF --Goteborg was given $7 million in the 1995 championships -- and soon the bills were running high.

Fouras and former SEGAS president Stratos Molivas spent a year publicly insulting each other on who was responsible for the mess and who had the upper hand in running event, putting all preparations virtually on hold.

"With about 10 months to go we had to rush to find suppliers and had no choice but to accept their high prices. They knew we were in need and in no position to negotiate," the championship's general manager Vangelis Savramis said.

One week before the start the Olympic Stadium still looks like a giant construction site with workers putting in new cabling, replacing broken chairs, painting interior walls and installing desks and telephone lines for the press.
"Things always take time in Greece but in the end it all works out fine. Right now I am under a lot of stress but I know that on August 1st I all will be fine," Fouras said.

The championship's financial failure is raising questions whether Greece can handle organising the Olympic Games. Yanna Daskalaki, the Athens 2004 bid committee president, has said if Athens wins the Games the cost would be $1.3 billion and revenue about $1.6 billion.
"If we get the Olympics I fear there will be widespread mismanagement of funds. Greeks will end up paying for years after the Games are held," Savramis said.
The championship, known as 'Athens 97', will be under scrutiny by some 40 visiting IOC members before the September 5 vote on which city will host the 2004 Olympics.

Almost all 110 IOC voting members will visit Greece within the next three weeks. They enjoy generous hospitality with luxury suites, limousine services with police excorts and meetings with senior government officials including Prime Minister Costas Simitis.
"I am against these extravagant services for IOC members. This effort to impress your visitor is not the best way to win the Olympics," Savramis said.
Athens, which lost the 1996 Games to Atlanta, is considered along with Rome the strongest bidders for the 2004 Olympic Games. The other three finalists are Stockholm, Cape Town and Buenos Aires.
